title: Ephemeral
body:
ephemeral (adjective): lasting for a very short time.

The word comes from the Greek ephemeros, meaning lasting only a day. Mayflies are the classic ephemeral creatures; some adults live for less than a day. Social media stories are ephemeral by design, disappearing after twenty-four hours.

title: Etymology
body:
etymology (noun): the study of the origin of words and the way their meanings have changed over time.

Etymology traces a word back through the languages it passed through. The English word etymology itself is borrowed from Greek etymon, the true sense of a word, by way of Latin and Old French.

title: Serendipity
body:
serendipity (noun): the occurrence of fortunate discoveries by accident.

The writer Horace Walpole coined serendipity in 1754, after a Persian fairy tale called The Three Princes of Serendip, whose heroes kept making lucky discoveries. Penicillin is often given as an example of serendipity in science.

title: Lexicon
body:
lexicon (noun): the vocabulary of a person, language, or branch of knowledge.

A lexicon is also a dictionary, especially of an ancient language such as Greek or Hebrew. Every specialist field builds its own lexicon; medicine and law are famous for theirs.

title: Where English vocabulary comes from
body:
English has borrowed words from many languages. After the Norman Conquest, French supplied a large share of the vocabulary of law, government, and food, which is why the animal is a cow but the meat is beef. Latin and Greek gave English much of its scientific vocabulary, while Norse settlers left everyday words such as sky, egg, and window.

A loanword is a word adopted from another language with little or no translation. Linguists estimate that well over half of the modern English lexicon has French or Latin roots, although the most frequent words remain Germanic.

title: Morpheme
body:
morpheme (noun): the smallest unit of a language that carries meaning.

The word unhappiness has three morphemes: the prefix un-, the root happy, and the suffix -ness. A free morpheme can stand alone as a word; a bound morpheme, like a plural suffix, cannot.
